I propose specifying executable IR semantics for allocation-site heaps, pointer casts, escapes, and opaque-call havoc, then validating with generated differential tests. Can we unpack what this proposal commits us to?

It commits to making those four areas of the intermediate representation precise enough to execute or otherwise evaluate as a defined semantic reference, then using generated differential tests to compare relevant behavior. The proposal is about specifying and validating the semantic basis of the alias analysis. It does not supply the rules themselves, a test-generation procedure, or any validation result.
Why emphasize executable semantics rather than just a prose description of the IR?

An executable specification makes its interpretations checkable on concrete generated cases. Prose documentation still matters, but an executable account can expose when two computations apply different interpretations of an allocation, cast, escape, or opaque call. The proposal does not say what form the executable specification takes or claim that making it executable automatically makes it complete.
Are we proposing to change what the IR means?

Not necessarily. The proposal is to specify executable IR semantics for the named cases so the analysis can be validated against a defined interpretation. It does not identify any existing IR rule to replace, introduce new cast behavior, or authorize a different meaning for opaque calls.
What does ‘allocation-site heaps’ mean at the level of this proposal?

It identifies allocation sites as the relevant basis for describing heap objects in the proposed semantics. The specification would need to make clear how allocations and heap-held pointer information contribute to alias reasoning. The node does not say whether individual allocations at the same site are distinguished in particular circumstances or prescribe a concrete heap-state representation.
Should I assume that two allocations from the same site always refer to the same concrete object?

No. An allocation-site abstraction used for analysis need not be identical to the identity of a concrete allocation. The proposal calls for executable semantics for allocation-site heaps, but it does not state a rule equating all concrete allocations from one site. That distinction would have to be made explicit in the specification rather than inferred from the phrase.
Is the executable semantics supposed to return alias answers directly?

That is not specified. It needs to define the behavior relevant to interpreting alias answers, including the named heap and pointer effects. The proposal does not require a particular query interface or say whether the executable semantics itself produces an alias matrix, a program-state result, or some other observable used in differential tests.
How much should the pointer-cast semantics say?

Enough to establish which pointer relationships casts may preserve, alter, or make relevant under the documented IR semantics. A differential comparison is ambiguous if one side silently treats a cast differently from the other. The proposal does not enumerate cast kinds or give their transfer rules, so we should not fill those rules in by assumption.
Could we simply say that every pointer cast is a no-op?

Only if that were actually justified by the IR semantics, and the proposal does not say it is. The executable specification must express the documented behavior, not choose a blanket rule for convenience. Likewise, the alias analysis must not discard a permitted relationship merely because a cast is involved.
What does specifying escapes add to the heap part?

Heap behavior describes objects and pointer information associated with them; escape behavior addresses when that information can matter outside the context in which it was produced. Specifying both helps establish which cross-function pointer effects the analysis must consider. The proposal does not give an escape definition or assert that every heap pointer escapes.
Is an escape just a label on a pointer, or does the proposal define its consequences?

The proposal does not choose a representation. For executable semantics to be useful, though, an escape must have a defined meaning for behavior that can affect alias reasoning, rather than being an unexplained label. Which operations create an escape and which effects follow remain to be specified according to the documented IR semantics.
How should I understand ‘opaque-call havoc’ without implying that every call changes everything?

It names conservative treatment of effects that an opaque call may have when its body is unavailable. The semantics should identify what such a call is permitted to affect, and havoc should account for possibilities that cannot be ruled out. The phrase alone does not specify that every opaque call modifies every object or that documented guarantees must be ignored.
Why use the word ‘havoc’ at all?

It conveys that unknown permitted effects cannot be treated as absent simply because their details are unavailable. The exact range of possible effects has to come from the IR semantics. Here ‘havoc’ is a proposed semantic treatment to specify, not a supplied list of memory locations or pointer relationships that an opaque call definitely changes.
Does opaque-call havoc make every resulting alias answer a ‘may alias’?

The proposal does not imply that. Soundness requires retaining possibilities allowed by the call’s documented semantics, but it does not require indiscriminately reporting every pointer pair as possibly aliasing when the semantics provides narrower guarantees. No precision result or effect boundary has been specified yet.
Could the executable semantics distinguish the fact that an opaque call may have an effect from a claim that it actually had that effect?

That distinction is important. A conservative semantic account can represent permitted alternatives without claiming every alternative occurs in each execution. The proposal does not state how alternatives are represented, but differential tests need an interpretation consistent with what the IR permits rather than an unsupported certainty about unknown behavior.
What are ‘generated differential tests’ intended to compare?

They are intended to expose differences between results produced under the specified IR semantics and results from the behavior being validated. For the incremental alias-analysis goal, a relevant comparison is post-edit alias answers against full recomputation for the same edited program, interpreted under the same documented semantics. The proposal does not fix the test oracle, generated-program language subset, or exact set of comparisons.
Does ‘generated’ imply random tests?

No. Generation describes how test cases are produced, not whether they are random, exhaustive, or constructed by a particular strategy. The proposal provides no generator design or test count, so none should be assumed.
Does differential testing by itself prove soundness?

No. It can reveal disagreements in cases that are generated and compared, and agreement can support confidence within that scope. It does not by itself prove that all programs and effects allowed by the documented IR semantics are handled soundly. The proposal is to validate with those tests, not to treat a finite set of matches as a universal proof.
Could two implementations agree with each other and still share the same mistaken interpretation of a cast?

Yes. Agreement is only as informative as the semantics and reference used to interpret it. Specifying executable IR semantics is meant to make the intended behavior explicit, but the executable specification itself still needs to reflect the documented IR rules. Differential agreement alone does not certify that the reference rules are correct.
Then what should we keep distinct when describing a successful differential test, if one occurs?

Keep three claims separate: what the documented IR permits, what the executable semantics encodes, and whether the compared analysis results agree on a generated case. The proposal supplies none of those test outcomes and does not establish that the executable account has already been checked against the documentation.
Would the tests need to exercise interactions among the four named areas, or can they treat each in isolation?

Interactions can matter conceptually: a cast may change which heap-held pointer information is relevant, an escape may let that information cross functions, and an opaque call may have permitted effects on it. The proposal does not prescribe a test matrix or require a particular combination in every case. Its stated scope includes allocation-site heaps, casts, escapes, and opaque-call havoc, whether considered individually or together.

It does not name indirect calls in its list of semantics to specify, although they remain part of the broader interprocedural alias-analysis goal. Heap-held pointers, casts, escapes, and opaque effects may be relevant to indirect-call reasoning, but we should not claim that this proposal alone specifies indirect-call target semantics or validates target changes.
And does allocation-site heap semantics settle recursion or SCC rebuilding?

No. Recursion remains a required soundness case, but this proposal focuses on the semantic treatment of the four named areas and generated differential validation. It does not specify recursive fixed-point computation, SCC rebuilding, or how changing function summaries are propagated after edits.

Yes. Generated cases can be used to compare the incremental and full-recomputation alias answers for the same edited program, provided their interpretation respects the specified IR semantics. The proposal does not give a match count, identify an edit set, or claim that such a comparison has been run.
Would a mismatch automatically tell us whether the fault lies in heap abstraction, cast semantics, escape handling, or opaque-call havoc?

No. A mismatch identifies a difference in the compared behavior. Diagnosing its cause could require examining how the named effects interact and whether the semantic reference or the analysis interpreted them as intended. The proposal reports neither a mismatch nor a diagnosis procedure.

No. Differential agreement concerns behavior on the generated comparisons; latency needs timing measurements. The broader goal is to match full recomputation’s alias answers after single-function edits while reducing median analysis latency by 50%. This proposal gives no latency measurement or numerical prediction.

Propose an executable specification of the documented IR semantics for allocation-site heaps, pointer casts, escapes, and opaque-call havoc, then validate relevant alias behavior with generated differential tests; the semantic rules, test outcomes, and latency results remain unspecified.
